entities.name: Quintus Lutatius Catulus Capitolinus
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Quintus Lutatius Catulus Capitolinus (c. 120 BC – 60 BC) was a prominent Roman statesman and military commander whose career spanned the tumultuous late Roman Republic, a period marked by civil strife and the gradual erosion of republican institutions. As a staunch Optimate, he embodied the conservative senatorial faction that sought to uphold traditional Roman governance against populist challenges. His most enduring significance stems from his pivotal role in defending the capital during the revolt of Marcus Aemilius Lepidus in 77 BC, an act that earned him the esteemed agnomen "Capitolinus" and cemented his reputation as a guardian of the Republic.

Catulus's political ascent included a praetorship by 81 BC, followed by his consulship in 78 BC alongside Lepidus, an alliance that quickly dissolved into civil conflict. Following Sulla's death, Lepidus attempted to repeal Sullan laws and marched on Rome, but Catulus, as proconsul, decisively repelled his forces in a series of engagements, notably at the Milvian Bridge and on the Capitoline Hill itself. His subsequent censorship in 65 BC, shared with Licinius Crassus, focused on public works and the moral oversight of the Roman citizenry, though it was marked by significant political disagreements, particularly regarding the enrollment of Transpadane Gauls as citizens.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Quintus Lutatius Catulus Capitolinus was a pivotal figure in the late Roman Republic, whose defense of Rome in 77 BC and subsequent architectural contributions significantly impacted the physical and political landscape of the capital. His consistent opposition to the ambitions of powerful generals helped define the conservative senatorial stance during a period of intense upheaval.
